q7.answer: The worker makes the 32-byte token, stores only its SHA-256 hash in password_reset_tokens, and puts the raw token only into the reset link in the email it sends through the mail provider. The raw token is never stored and never placed in a queue job, so the email is the only place it exists.

q8.answer: The API hashes the token from the URL with SHA-256 and looks up password_reset_tokens by token_hash, which is unique. The link is still good only if that row has used_at empty and expires_at later than now. No matching row gives the expired page, and a match gives the new-password form.

q9.answer: Each reset email request is one row in reset_sends with user_id and sent_at, indexed on (user_id, sent_at). The request handler counts that user's rows from the last hour while holding the user's row lock. Old requests drop out of the count by time, and rows older than one hour are purged.

q10.answer: Issuing a new link overwrites the account's single password_reset_tokens row with the new token_hash, which kills the earlier link. This happens in the worker's upsert, when the worker processes the new job, not when the request is made. The gap between request and worker run is a known open issue, and I did not decide whether it is acceptable or whether the worker should serialise upserts per user.

q11.answer: On a successful reset, one transaction marks the link used (atomic UPDATE), stores the new argon2id hash in users.password_hash, deletes all of the user's sessions rows, and adds the 'password changed' outbox job, then commits. The redirect to /login happens after the commit. The email is queued in that same transaction only if the queue is Postgres-backed, which is still an open question; otherwise it must be enqueued after COMMIT, with the risk of a missing email.

q12.answer: The link is burned by one atomic UPDATE that sets used_at = now() only where the hash matches and used_at is empty and expires_at is later than now. Postgres locks the row for the first UPDATE, so the second one waits and then re-checks the condition, finds used_at set, changes 0 rows, and gets the expired page. Only the first submission takes effect.
